summary:
This evaluation covered 8 investigation-type evals (one, "negative-unrelated-rds", was a should_trigger:false check that was fully skipped — both variants correctly did not need to produce findings there, so it offers no comparative signal) across 3 iterations each, with no run failures.

Trigger firing: Both variants' underlying trigger fired reliably (100% in 7/8 evals). One eval (e6-origin-outage-waf-cleared) only fired 2/3 times at the trigger level overall; without_skill's expected-output pass rate there was notably lower (1/3 vs with_skill's 3/3), and with_skill's output_consistency could not even be computed ("overall": null) for that eval, which limits confidence in that comparison.

Expected output / assertions: Across the evals with full data, with_skill met the expected-output bar at or near 100% in every eval, while without_skill was more variable — ranging from 100% (e5, e7) down to 67% (e2, e3) and 0% (e4, e6). At the assertion level, with_skill's pass rates were consistently equal to or higher than without_skill's in every eval (e.g., e4: 47% vs 13%; e7: 89% vs 39%; e1: 78% vs 67%), with without_skill never outperforming with_skill on aggregate assertion pass rate in any eval. Several individual assertions were "always_passes" for both variants (e.g., naming specific rule identifiers via regex in e1, e5, e7), meaning those checks don't discriminate between variants. A few assertions were "always_fails" for both (e.g., the Count-mode scoped rate-rule recommendation in e3/e4, the verbatim CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE token in e5), indicating those specific behaviors are weak spots for the agent type generally, not a difference between variants. Most other assertions were marked "flaky," meaning results varied by run for at least one variant, so single-run outcomes should be read cautiously; confidence on these LLM-graded assertions was mostly medium-to-high, with a few medium/low-confidence items (e.g., the "Caps confidence" and managed-rule-version assertions in e1/e7).

Quality comparison (pairwise LLM judging): Results were mixed and criterion-dependent. In e1, without_skill was favored slightly more often overall (6 vs 4, with 2 comparable); in e2 and e5, with_skill was favored more often (5 vs 3, and 5 vs 2 with 5 comparable, respectively); in e3, without_skill was favored more (7 vs 2); in e7, with_skill was favored strongly (9 vs 2). e4 and e6 had no quality pairs evaluated (all skipped), so no quality signal exists there. Confidence on these quality judgments was mostly medium, occasionally high.

Runtime and cost: with_skill was faster and cheaper in most evals (e.g., e1: 12m7s/$6.04 vs 18m11s/$9.06; e7: 12m54s/$6.43 vs 24m31s/$12.21), with one exception where without_skill was modestly faster/cheaper (e4: 11m50s/$5.89 vs with_skill's 12m16s/$6.12) and another (e5) where without_skill was faster (8m19s vs 11m5s) but also exceeded the runtime comparison threshold in all 3 pairs. These runtime/cost differences are a tradeoff dimension, not a quality verdict on their own, though in several evals with_skill's lower cost/runtime coincided with equal or higher assertion pass rates, which is a more favorable combination for with_skill there.

Output consistency: Both variants were generally "mostly_consistent" to "consistent" across evals, with similar scores in most cases (e.g., e2, e4, e5 nearly identical). with_skill reached "consistent" (highest rating) in e7, while without_skill was "mostly_consistent" there. In e6, without_skill was rated "inconsistent" (score 1.5) while with_skill's consistency could not be scored at all due to missing data.

Overall, across the dimensions measured, with_skill showed equal-or-higher expected-output and assertion pass rates in every eval with data, and was favored in quality comparisons in some evals (e2, e5, e7) while without_skill was favored in others (e1, e3); several individual assertions and whole quality comparisons were skipped or showed no discriminating signal, and some findings rest on flaky, run-to-run-variable, or lower-confidence assessments that temper how strongly any single result should be read.

e1-two-false-positives-one-window.summary:
This evaluation covers a single investigation task (WAF false-positive blocking incident) run 3 times per variant.

Trigger and expected output: Both variants fired the trigger and met the expected output on all 3 runs (100%), with high confidence in that judgment for both — this dimension shows no difference between variants.

Assertions (18 total per variant, across 6 distinct checks x 3 runs): with_skill passed 14/18 (78%) vs without_skill 12/18 (67%). Breaking this down:
- Two assertions always passed for both variants (naming both sub-rules; classifying matches as false positives, not an attack) — these are not differentiating since both variants handle them reliably.
- One assertion (no WAF config change caused the blocks) favored without_skill (3/3) over with_skill (2/3).
- One assertion (citing log/metric evidence per cause) favored with_skill (3/3) over without_skill (2/3, medium confidence).
- One assertion (separate Cause records per sub-rule, each with its own count/window) was flaky for both, but more so for without_skill (1/3 vs with_skill's 2/3).
- One assertion (explicitly ruling out managed rule group version changes) failed for both variants (with_skill 1/3, without_skill 0/3) — this indicates the behavior itself is weak or the bar is hard to meet for both, not a meaningful variant difference.
So the assertion-level picture is mixed: each variant has at least one assertion it handles better, and one shared weak spot.

Quality comparison (3 pairs evaluated, medium avg confidence): across all criteria combined, without_skill was favored in 6 instances, with_skill in 4, with 2 rated comparable. At the per-criterion level, impact_analysis_accuracy and supporting_evidence_quality leaned toward without_skill (2-1 each), while root_cause_accuracy and key_findings_accuracy were split evenly (1-1-1 comparable each). With only 3 pairs evaluated, these counts are based on a small sample and should be read as a mild lean toward without_skill's output quality rather than a decisive gap.

Runtime and cost: with_skill was notably faster (~12m7s vs ~18m11s) and cheaper (~$6.04 vs ~$9.06). Neither variant exceeded the runtime threshold in the 3 evaluated pairs. Context window utilization was low for both (with_skill 10.1%, without_skill 7.7%), with no compactions for either — not a meaningful difference.

Output consistency: both variants were rated "mostly_consistent" overall. with_skill scored slightly higher (2.5, with 2 dimensions fully "consistent" and 2 "mostly_consistent", medium confidence) versus without_skill (2.0, all 4 dimensions "mostly_consistent", high confidence). This suggests with_skill's outputs varied a bit less run-to-run, though the confidence levels differ (without_skill's rating is held with higher confidence despite the lower score).

Overall picture: this is a tradeoff rather than a clear-cut outcome. with_skill passed more assertions overall, ran faster and cheaper, and showed slightly more run-to-run consistency. without_skill showed a mild lean in favor on the quality-comparison criteria (though based on only 3 pairs) and performed better on the specific "no config change" assertion. Both variants shared a common weakness: failing to reliably rule out managed-rule-version changes as a possible cause, and both showed flakiness on the "separate Cause records" assertion — these point to areas needing improvement regardless of variant.

e6-origin-outage-waf-cleared.summary:
This single investigation-type eval looked at an incident RCA scenario involving a security-group change that caused timeouts, with an alternate hypothesis (AWS WAF) that was expected to be ruled out.

Trigger: the behavior under test fired in 2 of 3 runs overall (67%), so one of the three repeated runs may not provide fully comparable data for either variant.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in only 1 of 3 runs (33%, high confidence). Since confidence is high on both sides, this gap appears to be a real measured difference rather than a measurement artifact, though it rests on a small sample of 3 runs.

Assertions (12 checks across 4 criteria, each run 3 times): with_skill passed 11/12 (92%), without_skill passed 6/12 (50%). Looking at the four underlying criteria individually:
- Three criteria (naming the security-group change as root cause; tying both onset and recovery to the SG change/revert; citing supporting metric/CloudTrail evidence) were each passed 3/3 by with_skill but only 1/3 by without_skill — all three are flagged as "flaky" patterns, meaning results varied across repeated runs rather than being stable one way or the other.
- One criterion (correctly not blaming AWS WAF, or ruling it out with evidence) showed the reverse pattern: without_skill passed 3/3 while with_skill passed only 2/3 (medium confidence on with_skill's result). This assertion is also marked "flaky."
So no assertion passed uniformly for both variants, and no assertion failed for both; each had at least one gap, with with_skill weaker only on the WAF-attribution check and without_skill weaker on the other three.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 12m42s and $6.33 per run; without_skill averaged 15m45s and $7.85 per run. Variant_a was faster and cheaper by roughly 3 minutes and $1.52. Context window utilization was low for both (7.2% vs 9.4%) with no compaction events, so this wasn't a resource-strain factor for either.

Quality comparison: no pairs were actually evaluated head-to-head (0 of 3; all 3 were skipped), so there is no direct quality-comparison signal to weigh here.

Output consistency: with_skill's consistency was not measured (null). without_skill was rated "inconsistent" overall (score 1.5/4, with 2 of 4 dimensions "mostly consistent" and 2 "inconsistent"), at high confidence in that judgment. This aligns with the flaky, run-to-run variation seen in without_skill's assertion results, but because with_skill's consistency wasn't scored, we can't directly compare stability between the two.

Overall state: on this one eval, with_skill met the expected RCA conclusions more often and passed more assertions, while without_skill was notably more reliable at ruling out the WAF red herring. Variant_a was also somewhat faster and cheaper. However, the sample size is small (3 runs), several assertions show flaky/inconsistent behavior across runs for both variants, and the quality-comparison dimension produced no usable data at all. These gaps mean the measurements are informative but not highly robust, particularly for without_skill's reliability and for any head-to-head quality judgment.

However, confidence in that expected-output judgment was "high" for with_skill and only "medium" for without_skill, meaning the pass itself is more solidly established for with_skill and somewhat less certain for without_skill.

Assertions (per-run checks): This is where the clearest separation appears. Variant_b passed 16/18 assertion-instances (89%) vs without_skill's 7/18 (39%). Breaking it down by individual assertion:
- One assertion (about not blaming a Web ACL association/config change) passed 3/3 for both variants — this check doesn't differentiate them.

- One assertion (Gaps entry documenting denied Athena query permissions) passed 3/3 for with_skill and 0/3 for without_skill — a clean, consistent split rather than noise.
None of the assertions passed for neither variant, so the underlying checks appear meaningful rather than broken.

By criterion, key_findings_accuracy favored with_skill in all 3 pairs; root_cause_accuracy favored with_skill in 2 of 3 (1 comparable); impact_analysis_accuracy and supporting_evidence_quality each favored with_skill in 2 of 3, without_skill in 1 of 3. So without_skill did win on some individual quality comparisons, just less often.

Runtime and cost: Variant_b averaged ~12m54s and $6.43 per run; without_skill averaged ~24m31s and $12.21 — roughly double the time and cost. No runtime threshold violations occurred for either (0 of 3 pairs exceeded the 30s check used in the runtime comparison). Context window utilization was low and similar for both (13.4% vs 15.4%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency across repeated runs: Variant_b was rated "consistent" (score 3.0, high confidence) across all 4 consistency dimensions, while without_skill was "mostly_consistent" (score 2.0, medium confidence) across its 4 dimensions — indicating without_skill's outputs varied somewhat more run-to-run, and that this assessment itself carries slightly less confidence than with_skill's.

Overall picture: Across assertions, quality comparisons, and consistency, with_skill shows higher pass rates and more favorable quality judgments in this eval, while also running faster and at lower cost. Variant_a still met the basic expected-output bar every time and won a minority of individual quality/assertion comparisons, so it is not a uniform failure — but the combination of lower assertion pass rate, more quality criteria favoring with_skill, higher cost/runtime, and lower run-to-run consistency are all pointing in the same direction for without_skill in this particular eval.
